sections.title: Section 1: Hiring a room for a party
sections.instructions: Questions 1-10. Complete the form below. Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer. For Questions 9 and 10, choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

script.speaker: Woman
script.text: Good morning, Hillview Community Hall, Sandra speaking. How can I help you?

script.speaker: Man
script.text: Hello. I'm calling because I'd like to hire a room for a family party next month. Is that something you do?

script.speaker: Woman
script.text: Yes, of course. We have three rooms available for private hire. Can I start by taking a few details?

script.speaker: Man
script.text: Sure.

script.speaker: Woman
script.text: What's your name, please?

script.speaker: Man
script.text: It's David Ogunleye.

script.speaker: Woman
script.text: Could you spell the surname for me?

script.speaker: Man
script.text: Yes, it's O-G-U-N-L-E-Y-E.

script.speaker: Woman
script.text: O-G-U-N-L-E-Y-E. Thank you, Mr Ogunleye. And is there a phone number we can reach you on?

script.speaker: Man
script.text: My mobile is 07946 318205.

script.speaker: Woman
script.text: 07946 318205. Lovely. And what kind of event is it?

script.speaker: Man
script.text: It's my mother's seventieth birthday. We're planning a lunch with the family and some of her old friends from church.

script.speaker: Woman
script.text: How lovely. And what date were you thinking of?

script.speaker: Man
script.text: Saturday the 18th of May, if possible. I know it's quite short notice.

script.speaker: Woman
script.text: Let me just check the calendar. Saturday the 18th... yes, we still have availability that day. How many guests are you expecting?

script.speaker: Man
script.text: About sixty, I think. Maybe a few more if my cousins come from Manchester.

script.speaker: Woman
script.text: Right. In that case the Garden Room would be too small, because it only holds forty. I'd suggest either the Main Hall, which takes up to a hundred and twenty people, or the Lakeside Room, which holds seventy.

script.speaker: Man
script.text: What's the difference, apart from the size?

script.speaker: Woman
script.text: The Main Hall has a stage and a sound system, so it's popular for weddings and dances. The Lakeside Room is smaller, but it has large windows looking over the water and doors that open onto a terrace.

script.speaker: Man
script.text: The Lakeside Room sounds perfect. My mother loves being outside. How much is it?

script.speaker: Woman
script.text: On a Saturday, the Lakeside Room is forty-five pounds an hour. Most people book it for at least four hours.

script.speaker: Man
script.text: We'd need it from twelve until five, so that's five hours.

script.speaker: Woman
script.text: That would come to two hundred and twenty-five pounds. There's also a refundable deposit of one hundred pounds, which we return as long as the room is left clean and nothing is damaged.

script.speaker: Man
script.text: That's fine. What about food? Are we allowed to bring our own?

script.speaker: Woman
script.text: You are. Some people use our recommended caterer, but you're welcome to bring your own food. The room has a small kitchen with a fridge and a microwave, but there's no oven, I'm afraid.

script.speaker: Man
script.text: That's OK. My sisters are cooking, so we'll bring everything ready to serve. Do you provide plates and cutlery?

script.speaker: Woman
script.text: We do, and there's no extra charge for those. Tablecloths are extra, though. They're two pounds each.

script.speaker: Man
script.text: We'll bring our own tablecloths, then. What about decorations? My nieces want to put up balloons and banners.

script.speaker: Woman
script.text: Decorations are fine, but please don't use anything that sticks to the walls, like tape. There are hooks along the walls that you can hang things from. And candles aren't allowed, I'm afraid, for safety reasons, even on the birthday cake.

script.speaker: Man
script.text: Oh, that's a shame, but I understand. And parking? Some of the guests are elderly.

script.speaker: Woman
script.text: There's a car park right behind the building with about thirty spaces, and it's free at weekends. There are also two disabled spaces right next to the entrance.

script.speaker: Man
script.text: Great. So how do I confirm the booking?

script.speaker: Woman
script.text: I'll post a booking form to your home address, and you'll need to pay the deposit within seven days to secure the date. The rest is due two weeks before the event.

script.speaker: Man
script.text: Can I pay by card?

script.speaker: Woman
script.text: Yes, either by card over the phone or by bank transfer.

script.speaker: Man
script.text: Lovely. Oh, one more thing. What time can we get in to set up?

script.speaker: Woman
script.text: The room's booked from twelve, but if nobody is using it before you, we can let you in half an hour early at no extra cost. I'll make a note of that on your booking.

script.speaker: Man
script.text: That's really kind. Thank you so much for your help.

script.speaker: Woman
script.text: You're welcome. I hope your mother has a wonderful day.

sections.title: Section 2: Oakridge Heritage Village
sections.instructions: Questions 11-20. For Question 11 and Questions 17-20, choose the correct letter, A, B or C. For Questions 12-16, choose the correct activity, A-G, for each place.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Oakridge Heritage Village. My name's Peter, and I'll be giving you a short introduction before you set off to explore on your own. The village is an open-air museum, which means that instead of keeping everything in glass cases, we've rebuilt more than twenty historic buildings from around the region, and you're free to walk in and out of them. Most of them were brought here piece by piece from their original locations, with every brick and beam numbered, and then put back together exactly as they were.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: At the moment you're standing in the visitor centre. If you look at the map in your leaflet, you'll see that the village is laid out along one main street, with the river on your left as you walk down it. I'd like to tell you about a few buildings that have something special going on today.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: The first building you'll come to is the bakery. It dates from around 1880, and it still has its original brick oven. Our bakers light it at seven every morning, and from about eleven o'clock you can buy bread and buns made to traditional recipes. They tend to sell out by early afternoon, so don't leave it too late.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: Further along on the right is the blacksmith's workshop. Our blacksmith, Joe, gives demonstrations there throughout the day, but for safety reasons visitors have to stay behind the rope barrier. Children love watching the sparks, but please keep them close to you. Joe is also happy to answer questions once he's finished working on a piece.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: Opposite the blacksmith's you'll find the schoolhouse. This is one of the most popular buildings with families. At half past eleven and again at two o'clock, one of our volunteers dresses up as a Victorian teacher and runs a lesson. Children sit at the old wooden desks and practise writing on slates. Be warned, the teacher is very strict! Adults are welcome to join in too, although there are only thirty seats, so arrive early if you want one.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: At the end of the street, beside the river, is the water mill. It's the oldest building on the site, and parts of it are over three hundred years old. The wheel is turning today, and inside you can see how grain was ground into flour. The upper floor of the mill is closed at the moment while we repair the staircase, but the ground floor is open as usual.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: Finally, if you cross the small bridge, you'll come to the farmhouse. Here you can try your hand at some traditional crafts, and today we're running a basket-weaving workshop. It's free, but you'll need to pick up a ticket here at the visitor centre, because numbers are limited to twelve per session.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: Now, a few practical points. Toilets are located in the visitor centre and behind the farmhouse. If you'd like something to eat, the tea room is next to the bakery and serves hot meals until three. You're also welcome to bring your own food, and there are picnic tables on the grass beside the river. We do ask that you don't feed the animals in the farmyard, as they're on a special diet.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: The village closes at five o'clock, but the last entry to the buildings is at half past four, so please plan your visit with that in mind. Photography is allowed everywhere except inside the schoolhouse during lessons, because some of our volunteers prefer not to be photographed. And if you're thinking of coming back, our annual pass costs only twice the price of a single ticket, and you can upgrade today by showing your ticket at the shop.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: Right, that's everything from me. Enjoy your visit, and if you have any questions, our staff are all wearing green jackets, so they're easy to spot.

sections.title: Section 3: Student travel survey tutorial
sections.instructions: Questions 21-30. For Question 21, write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER. For Questions 22-26, choose the correct letter, A, B or C. For Questions 27-30, choose the correct letter, A-D.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: Come in, both of you, and take a seat. So, you're here to talk about your project for the human geography module. Remind me what you've chosen.

script.speaker: Amina
script.text: We're looking at how students travel to the campus. We want to find out which forms of transport people use and why, and then suggest ways the university could encourage more sustainable travel.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: Good, that's a very practical topic. How far have you got?

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: Well, we've done a first round of data collection. We stood at the three main entrances for three mornings, between eight and ten, and counted everyone arriving, and we also asked a sample of students how long their journey had taken.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: And what did you find?

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: On average, the journey took about thirty-five minutes. The thing that surprised us most was that the most common way of arriving wasn't the bus, as we'd expected, but walking.

script.speaker: Amina
script.text: We think that's because so many students now rent rooms in the streets close to the campus, rather than living in the city centre.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: That's an interesting hypothesis. How are you going to test it?

script.speaker: Amina
script.text: We were going to do a questionnaire. We've drafted about twenty questions so far.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: Twenty is quite a lot for a survey you're handing out at the entrance. People are on their way to lectures and won't want to spend more than a few minutes. I'd cut it down to eight or ten at most, and make most of them multiple choice so they're quick to answer.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: OK, that makes sense. We also thought about interviewing the university's transport officer.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: Definitely do that. She'll be able to tell you things you can't observe, like how many parking permits are issued and what the bus companies have agreed to. Have you contacted her yet?

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: Not yet.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: I'd do it soon. She's extremely busy at the moment because the new parking charges start next month, so her diary will fill up quickly.

script.speaker: Amina
script.text: There was one problem with our data. On the third morning there was a rail strike, so a lot more people drove or got lifts, and we're not sure whether to include those figures.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: What's your instinct?

script.speaker: Amina
script.text: I think we should leave them out, because it wasn't a typical day.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: But I think they're still useful. Strikes and road closures happen quite often, so it's part of reality.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: You could do both. Present the results with and without that day, and explain the difference. That's actually a more sophisticated approach, and it shows the examiners you've thought carefully about your data.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: Good idea.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: Now, what about your reading? What sources have you looked at?

script.speaker: Amina
script.text: We found a national travel survey published by the government, which has lots of statistics.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: That's useful for background, but remember that it covers the whole population, and students behave quite differently. You need something closer to your own context. Have you looked at studies from other universities?

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: We found one from a university in the Netherlands where they introduced free bike hire for students, and car use dropped by nearly a third in two years.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: Excellent, that's exactly the kind of thing you need. You could compare their situation with ours. Right, let's talk about dividing up the work. There's quite a lot to do before the presentation.

script.speaker: Amina
script.text: I'm happy to redesign the questionnaire, since I wrote the first draft.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: Fine. And the interview with the transport officer?

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: I'll do that. I sat on the students' union transport committee last year, so I know what to ask.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: Good. Who's going to write the literature review?

script.speaker: Amina
script.text: Me, I think. I've already started reading.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: And what about the slides?

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: We thought we'd do those together at the end, once everything else is finished.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: Sensible. And I'll book the seminar room with the projector for you, because students can't reserve it themselves. Any final questions?

script.speaker: Amina
script.text: How long should the presentation be?

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: Fifteen minutes, plus five for questions. Don't go over, because timing is part of the mark.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: Thanks, that's really helpful.

sections.title: Section 4: Lecture on sleep in animals
sections.instructions: Questions 31-40. Complete the notes below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer. For Questions 38 and 40, choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Good afternoon. In today's lecture I want to look at a question that has puzzled biologists for a very long time: why do animals sleep, and why do different species sleep in such different ways?

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Let's start with a definition, because that's less obvious than it sounds. Scientists generally identify sleep by a set of behaviours rather than by what's happening inside the brain, since we can't attach electrodes to every animal we want to study. An animal is considered to be asleep if it is inactive, if it usually adopts a particular posture, and, most importantly, if it is less responsive to its surroundings, so that it takes a stronger stimulus to get a reaction. Crucially, unlike an animal that is unconscious, a sleeping animal can be woken up fairly quickly.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Using this definition, we find sleep, or something very like it, almost everywhere we look. Mammals and birds sleep, of course, but so do reptiles, fish and even insects. Fruit flies, for example, have periods of rest during which they're much harder to disturb, and if you keep them awake, they'll rest for longer the next day to make up for it, which is exactly what we do after a late night. Researchers call this sleep rebound, and it's one of the strongest pieces of evidence that sleep is a genuine need rather than simply a way of passing time.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: So how much sleep do animals need? The range is enormous. Some species of bat sleep for around twenty hours a day, while giraffes and elephants may sleep for only three or four. One pattern that has emerged is that large plant-eating animals tend to sleep less. The usual explanation is food: grass and leaves contain relatively little energy, so these animals have to spend most of their waking hours eating. Being asleep also makes them vulnerable to predators, which is another reason to keep it short.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Some of the most fascinating cases involve animals that simply can't afford to switch off completely. Dolphins and some other marine mammals have to come to the surface regularly to breathe, so total unconsciousness would be dangerous. Their solution is what's known as unihemispheric sleep, in which one half of the brain sleeps while the other half stays awake. They usually keep open the eye that is connected to the waking half of the brain, which helps them watch for threats and stay in contact with the group.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Birds can do something similar. Ducks sleeping in a row have been observed keeping one eye open, and it's the birds at the ends of the row, in the most exposed positions, that do this most often. Even more remarkable is a study of frigatebirds, large seabirds that can stay in the air for weeks at a time over the ocean. By recording their brain activity during flight, researchers found that they do sleep while flying, sometimes with one half of the brain and sometimes with both. But they sleep for less than an hour a day in the air, compared with more than twelve hours a day when they're back on land.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: That brings us to the big question: what is sleep actually for? There are several theories. One is energy conservation, the idea that sleeping reduces the amount of energy an animal uses during periods when it can't feed efficiently. Another, which has received a lot of attention recently, is that sleep allows the brain to clear away waste products that build up during waking hours. A third theory links sleep to memory: during sleep, the brain seems to strengthen important connections formed during the day and weaken less useful ones.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: These theories aren't really in competition. Most researchers now believe that sleep probably serves several functions at once, and that the balance between them may differ from species to species. That's partly why studying unusual sleepers like frigatebirds is so valuable: they show us what is absolutely essential and what can be given up when necessary.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: For next week, I'd like you to read the chapter on sleep in the course textbook, and we'll be looking in more detail at human sleep cycles.

sections.title: Section 1: Renting a storage unit
sections.instructions: Questions 1-10. Complete the form below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer, or choose the correct letter.

script.speaker: Woman
script.text: Good morning, SafeKeep Storage, Lucy speaking. How can I help you?

script.speaker: Man
script.text: Hi there. I'm calling because I'd like to rent a storage unit. I'm moving out of my flat at the end of the month, and my new place won't be ready until later in the year, so I need somewhere to keep my things for a while.

script.speaker: Woman
script.text: No problem at all. I'll just take a few details first, and then I can tell you what we've got available. Could I have your name, please?

script.speaker: Man
script.text: Yes, it's Daniel Okonkwo.

script.speaker: Woman
script.text: And could you spell your surname for me?

script.speaker: Man
script.text: Sure. It's O-K-O-N-K-W-O.

script.speaker: Woman
script.text: Thank you, Mr Okonkwo. And what's the best number to contact you on?

script.speaker: Man
script.text: My mobile is probably best. It's 07832 559 104.

script.speaker: Woman
script.text: Let me read that back: 07832 559 104.

script.speaker: Man
script.text: That's right.

script.speaker: Woman
script.text: And your current address?

script.speaker: Man
script.text: It's 14 Harcourt Road, and the postcode is BR3 6TN.

script.speaker: Woman
script.text: BR3 6TN. Lovely. Now, can you tell me roughly how much you need to store?

script.speaker: Man
script.text: It's basically everything from a one-bedroom flat. So there's a double bed, a sofa, a small dining table with four chairs, a fridge, and maybe twenty or so boxes of books and clothes.

script.speaker: Woman
script.text: OK. For that amount I wouldn't recommend our small unit, which is really just for boxes. The large unit would be far more than you need, so I'd suggest the medium unit. It's about the size of a single garage.

script.speaker: Man
script.text: That sounds about right. How much does that cost?

script.speaker: Woman
script.text: The medium unit is normally £32 a week, but we have a special offer this month, so it's £28 a week.

script.speaker: Man
script.text: And is there any reduction if I rent it for a longer period? I think I'll need it for about four months.

script.speaker: Woman
script.text: Yes, there is. If you book for twelve weeks or more, you get 20 percent off the weekly price. So with four months you'd qualify for that.

script.speaker: Man
script.text: Great. And when could I start? I'm planning to move my things on a Saturday.

script.speaker: Woman
script.text: We have medium units free from next week. Which date were you thinking of?

script.speaker: Man
script.text: Well, the removal company is booked for the 18th of June.

script.speaker: Woman
script.text: The 18th of June. That's fine, I'll reserve a unit from that date.

script.speaker: Man
script.text: Do I need insurance for the contents?

script.speaker: Woman
script.text: Lastly, when you come in on the first day, please bring some proof of identity, like a passport or driving licence, and a recent utility bill.

script.speaker: Man
script.text: No problem. Thanks very much for your help.

sections.title: Section 2: Volunteering at Riverside Community Library
sections.instructions: Questions 11-14: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C. Questions 15-20: What will volunteers do in each area of the library? Choose SIX answers from the list, A-G.

script.speaker: Coordinator
script.text: Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming along to this information session. My name is Grace Mensah and I'm the volunteer coordinator here at the new Riverside Community Library. Tonight I'm going to tell you a little about the building, and then explain the different volunteer roles we're hoping to fill.

script.speaker: Coordinator
script.text: First, a bit of background. The library opened in March, after nearly two years of construction. A lot of people assume it was built on the site of the old textile factory, but in fact the factory stood across the road, where the new flats are now. This site was previously a bus depot, and if you look carefully at the entrance you can still see some of the original brick arches, which the architects decided to keep.

script.speaker: Coordinator
script.text: The building has some unusual environmental features. The original plans included solar panels on the roof, but these were dropped because of the cost. Instead, the roof was turned into a garden where volunteers and local schoolchildren grow vegetables, which are then given to the food bank next door. It's become one of the most popular parts of the building.

script.speaker: Coordinator
script.text: Now, what do we ask of our volunteers? When we first advertised, we asked people to commit to at least three months, but we found that put a lot of people off, so we've dropped that requirement. What we do ask is that you give a minimum of two hours a week, and that you let us know in advance if you can't come.

script.speaker: Coordinator
script.text: All new volunteers attend a training session before they start. We used to run these on Saturday mornings, but they clashed with our busiest time, and Monday evenings didn't suit people with young children. So training now takes place on Wednesday afternoons, from two until five. If that's impossible for you, speak to me afterwards and we'll try to arrange something.

script.speaker: Coordinator
script.text: Right, let me go through the main areas of the library and what volunteers do in each one.

script.speaker: Coordinator
script.text: On the ground floor you'll find the children's zone. The staff there run the lending desk and the craft activities, but what we really need from volunteers is people to read stories aloud to the under-fives, especially during our morning sessions for parents and toddlers.

script.speaker: Coordinator
script.text: Next to that is the digital hub, which has thirty computers. Many of our older visitors have never used a computer before, so volunteers sit with them and help them do things like send emails, apply for jobs online or video-call relatives abroad.

script.speaker: Coordinator
script.text: Moving up to the first floor, there are the study rooms. Every weekday from four o'clock, these fill up with secondary school students, and volunteers support them with their homework, particularly maths and science. You don't need to be a teacher, just patient and reasonably confident with the subject.

script.speaker: Coordinator
script.text: Also on the first floor is the community archive. This is a project I'm particularly excited about. Volunteers meet long-time residents of the area and record their oral histories, their memories of how the neighbourhood has changed, so that future generations can listen to them.

script.speaker: Coordinator
script.text: In the basement, there's the sorting room. We receive hundreds of donated books every month, and volunteers there organise them, checking their condition and deciding whether they go onto the shelves or to our charity sales.

script.speaker: Coordinator
script.text: And finally, on the top floor, next to the roof garden, we have the language café. Every Thursday evening, people who are learning English come along, and volunteers chat with them over tea and coffee, so they can practise their conversation in a relaxed setting.

script.speaker: Coordinator
script.text: Some of you have asked about school tours. We do get lots of visits from local schools, but those tours are led by our professional staff, so they're not a volunteer role.

script.speaker: Coordinator
script.text: OK, I'll stop there and take some questions.

sections.title: Section 3: A research project on canteen food waste
sections.instructions: Questions 21-24: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C. Questions 25-30: Who will be responsible for each task? Choose A, B or C.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: Come in, Chidi, Hannah. So, you wanted to talk about your research project on food waste in the university canteen. How's it going?

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: Pretty well, I think. We've done the pilot study and we've got a few questions about the next stage.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: Good. Remind me first why you chose this topic. I know there's already quite a lot of published research on household food waste.

script.speaker: Chidi
script.text: That's true, but it was really Hannah's idea. She works part-time in the canteen on weekends.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: Yes, and every Saturday I'd see bins full of food that had hardly been touched. I just kept wondering why students were throwing so much away, so it felt like something worth investigating.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: That's a good starting point. Personal experience can be a strong motivation. So, what did the pilot study tell you?

script.speaker: Chidi
script.text: Well, the main thing we learned was about our questionnaire. We gave it to twenty students, and most of them gave up halfway through. It was just far too long, so we've cut it from forty questions to fifteen.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: We also looked at what kind of food was thrown away. We expected rice to be the biggest category, but actually it was vegetables.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: Interesting. And had you compared lunch and dinner?

script.speaker: Chidi
script.text: Not yet. We only collected data at lunchtime in the pilot.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: OK. Now, for the main study, how many students are you planning to survey?

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: About a hundred and fifty. We wondered if we should try to get more.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: Actually, a hundred and fifty is plenty for a project of this size. What I'd suggest instead is collecting your data over a longer period, at least four weeks rather than one. The canteen menu rotates, so if you only look at one week, the results may just reflect what happened to be served that week.

script.speaker: Chidi
script.text: That makes sense. We hadn't thought about the menu.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: We also want to weigh the food left on plates. Do you see any problems with that?

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: Hygiene isn't really an issue as long as you wear gloves, and I don't think the time involved will be a problem if you do it in shifts. The main thing is that you'll need written permission from the catering manager before you start. Without that, you can't go behind the counter.

script.speaker: Chidi
script.text: Right, we'll email her this week.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: Good. Now, have you decided how you're dividing up the work?

script.speaker: Chidi
script.text: Mostly. Hannah's going to redesign the questionnaire, since she wrote the first version.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: And Chidi's going to do the weighing, because he has more free time at lunchtime than I do.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: What about interviewing the kitchen staff?

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: I'll do that. I know most of them already, so they'll probably be more relaxed talking to me.

script.speaker: Chidi
script.text: And I'll take care of the statistical analysis. I did a course on that software last year.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: And the literature review?

script.speaker: Chidi
script.text: We were going to split it, but in the end we thought it would be more consistent if we worked on it together, reading the same articles and discussing them.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: That's sensible. And the final presentation?

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: I'm going to prepare that. Chidi's not keen on designing slides.

script.speaker: Chidi
script.text: It's true. I'll proofread it, though.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: Good. It sounds as though you're well organised. Just make sure you agree on deadlines for each stage, and keep a shared record of any changes you make to the plan, so neither of you is surprised later on. Let's meet again in three weeks to see how the data collection is going.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: Thanks. That's been really useful.

sections.title: Section 4: Urban heat islands
sections.instructions: Questions 31-33: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C. Questions 34-40: Complete the notes below. Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Good morning. In today's lecture in our series on urban environments, I'm going to look at a phenomenon known as the urban heat island. Put simply, this is the tendency for cities to be noticeably warmer than the countryside around them. On a calm, clear night, the centre of a large city can be as much as ten degrees Celsius warmer than nearby farmland.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: The effect was first described in the early nineteenth century by an amateur scientist called Luke Howard, who kept careful temperature records in and around London. Interestingly, Howard is better remembered today for something else entirely: he was the man who gave clouds the names we still use, such as cumulus and stratus. But his observation that the city was consistently warmer than the surrounding villages was the beginning of a whole field of research.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: So why does this happen? There are several causes. The first relates to the materials cities are built from. Concrete, brick and especially asphalt absorb a great deal of energy from the sun during the day and then release it slowly at night. That's why the difference between city and countryside is usually greatest after sunset, not in the middle of the afternoon, as many people assume.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: A second cause is the shape of the city itself. Tall buildings on either side of a narrow street create what researchers call an urban canyon. Heat that would normally escape into the sky is trapped between the walls, and the buildings also reduce wind speed, so there's less movement of air to carry the warmth away.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Third, there's the lack of vegetation. In rural areas, plants release water through their leaves in a process called evapotranspiration, which has a cooling effect, a bit like sweating does for the human body. When land is covered in roads and buildings, this natural cooling largely disappears.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Finally, cities generate a great deal of waste heat from vehicles, factories and air-conditioning units. And air conditioning creates a vicious circle: the hotter the city becomes, the more people use it, and the more heat is pumped out into the streets.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Why does all this matter? The most serious consequence is for health. During heatwaves, death rates in cities rise sharply, and elderly people living alone are particularly at risk. There are also economic costs, mainly through higher demand for electricity, and environmental ones, since warmer air speeds up the formation of ground-level ozone, a harmful pollutant.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: What can be done? One of the simplest solutions is to change the colour of surfaces. So-called cool roofs, which are painted white or covered in reflective material, can reduce the temperature of a roof by over twenty degrees on a sunny day. Several cities are now experimenting with lighter-coloured road surfaces as well.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: A second approach is to bring back vegetation. Planting street trees is especially effective, because trees provide shade as well as cooling through evapotranspiration. Some cities have also introduced green roofs, which are covered in plants. These are more expensive than cool roofs, but they have the added benefit of absorbing rainwater, which reduces the risk of flooding.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Lastly, urban planners are paying more attention to the layout of new developments, for example by designing wide streets that line up with the direction of the prevailing wind, creating what are sometimes called ventilation corridors.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: In the next part of the lecture, we'll look at a case study of one city that has used all three approaches.
